newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian synagogue unites Jews, Christians, Moslems.
newsitem.headline: Russian synagogue unites Jews, Christians, Moslems.

text.p: In a wood under the shadow of a monument to millions killed in World War Two, Jews laid the foundation of a new synagogue and claimed their place alongside Christians and Moslems in Russian history on Tuesday.

Russian Jews with thick beards, dressed in black top coats and flat black hats, sat next to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin who helped lay the foundation of the first new synagogue in Moscow since the Bolshevik revolution in 1917.

The synagogue will stand on the far side of Russia's World War Two Victory Park from an Orthodox Church, and a mosque will be built close by. The aim is to unite the three religions and citizens who fought together against Nazi Germany.

"In this country, 55 years ago, my family, 113 people, were killed in a forest like this by the Nazis," said Israel Singer, secretary-general of the World Jewish Congress, who came to Russia for the foundation laying.
"We have come to thank the people of Russia for making us feel at home."
Jews have faced strident anti-Semitism for centuries in Russia and thousands battled to emigrate in the 1970s.
There are only three synagogues in Moscow, which has a Jewish population of 200,000 to 250,000 people, community leaders say.
Between 1.5 and two million Jews are known to live in Russia, though leaders say many more who renounced or hid their identity during the Soviet era are beginning to reclaim their religion.
Tankred Golenpolsky, publisher of Moscow's International Jewish Gazette, said that a local rabbi, a Moslem cleric and an Orthodox priest planned to hold a joint ceremony in Moscow.
Israel's ambassador to Russia, Aliza Shenhar said: "Let this synagogue, next to the church and mosque, strengthen the bond between peoples and religions."
The new synagogue was caught in a whirlwind of events, including last year's 50th anniversary of the end of World War Two, Moscow's 850th anniversary and the emergence of democracy in Russia.
Government officials focused on the contribution of Jews during the war, the memory of which is still a powerful uniting force in Russia, which lost over 26 million people in the war.
Chernomyrdin called for an end to anti-Semitism and, saying only a unified Russia could live happily, added that all Russians had to acknowledge the contribution of Jews to the motherland.
"When every third person died, no one has the right to forget, not a single person," he said. Almost one third of Russian Jews were killed during World War Two.
"This will be a memorial to the Jewish soldiers whom we met in every unit," said Moscow Deputy Mayor Valery Shantsev.
Jewish leaders said the synagogue would not have been possible before democracy in Russia and would be the beginning of a renaissance of Jewish culture as Russians and Jews learned to live together.
"The war touched almost every family... not only Jews, not only Russians," said Russian Jewish Congress president, Vladimir Gusinsky, also chairman of powerful Most Bank.
He said the Congress hoped to build cultural centres across Russia to reawaken Russia's Jewish cultural heritage.
Some Jewish leaders said Russia's prominent support of the synagogue was a sign that the country acknowledged its mistakes.
"It was a way of saying I'm sorry," said Golenpolsky.
